questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which amino acid's side chain is most useful for buffering near physiological pH (7.4)?
questions.explain: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa of about 6.0, closer to 7.4 than any other side chain, so it's meaningfully both protonated and deprotonated near physiological pH.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A competitive enzyme inhibitor primarily:
questions.explain: Competitive inhibitors compete with substrate for the active site, enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor, so Vmax is reachable, just at a higher apparent Km.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: The isoelectric point (pI) of a peptide is the pH at which its net charge is:
questions.explain: pI is defined as the pH where positive and negative charges on the molecule exactly balance, so neither the acidic nor the basic groups win, and the molecule stops moving in an electric field.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Km represents the substrate concentration at which reaction velocity equals:
questions.explain: By definition, when [S] = Km, v = Vmax/2, Km is a measure of apparent affinity, not a rate itself.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which of these amino acids has an acidic side chain?
questions.explain: Aspartate's side chain is a carboxylic acid, deprotonated (negatively charged) at physiological pH, one of only two acidic standard amino acids, along with glutamate.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which one-letter code corresponds to Tryptophan?
questions.explain: T was already taken by Threonine, so Tryptophan got W instead, one of the nine amino acids whose code doesn't match its first letter.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which two amino acids are the only purely ketogenic ones?
questions.explain: Only leucine and lysine cannot contribute any carbon to glucose. Both begin with L, which is the whole mnemonic. Every other amino acid is glucogenic or both.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which level of protein structure is held together by peptide bonds?
questions.explain: Primary structure is the covalent sequence itself. Secondary structure comes from backbone hydrogen bonds, tertiary from side chain interactions, and quaternary from separate subunits assembling.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: At what pH is the net charge on an amino acid zero?
questions.explain: The pH where positive and negative charges balance is a property of that molecule's own set of ionizable groups. It is not generally 7, and it is not the same as any single pKa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, what does the y-intercept give you?
questions.explain: The double reciprocal plot puts 1/Vmax at the y-intercept and -1/Km at the x-intercept. That is the whole reason it was used before nonlinear fitting was easy.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Which inhibition type lowers both Km and Vmax?
questions.explain: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds only the enzyme-substrate complex. Removing ES pulls the binding equilibrium forward, which lowers apparent Km while also capping Vmax.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: kcat/Km is best described as a measure of what?
questions.explain: kcat/Km combines how fast the enzyme turns over with how well it captures substrate, which is why it is the number used to compare enzymes against each other.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A protein is at a pH above its pI. What is its net charge?
questions.explain: Above the pI there are more deprotonated acidic groups than protonated basic ones, which is what makes a protein bind an anion exchange column rather than a cation one.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: How many of the 20 standard amino acids have an ionizable side chain?
questions.explain: Seven: aspartate, glutamate, histidine, cysteine, tyrosine, lysine and arginine. In pKa order they spell DEHCYKR, and they are the only ones that change a protein's charge.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Noncompetitive inhibition affects Vmax and Km how?
questions.explain: A pure noncompetitive inhibitor binds enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex equally well, so it removes functional enzyme without changing how tightly substrate binds.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Tris shifts about -0.028 pH units per degree C. If you set a Tris buffer to pH 8.00 at 25 C, what is it in a 4 C cold room?
questions.explain: Cooling by 21 degrees raises the pH by roughly 21 x 0.028, which is about 0.59 units. This is why Tris buffers should be adjusted at the temperature where they will be used.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A peptide has 2 Asp, 1 Lys, a free N terminus and a free C terminus, and no other ionizable groups. What is its approximate net charge at pH 7.0?
questions.explain: Count groups, not residues. The two Asp side chains and the C terminus are each about -1 at pH 7, while the N terminus and the Lys side chain are each about +1, so three negatives against two positives leaves one net negative.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A dipeptide has a free N terminus (pKa 9.0), a free C terminus (pKa 3.1) and one Lysine side chain (pKa 10.53). What is its approximate pI?
questions.explain: Two bases against one acid means the molecule is still positive at neutral pH, so the zero crossing has to sit high, between the two pKa values that bracket it. Averaging the two lowest pKa values is the usual mistake and lands near 6.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: HEPES has a pKa of 7.55 at 25 C and a temperature coefficient of -0.014 per degree C. What is its pKa at 4 C?
questions.explain: A negative coefficient means the pKa falls as temperature rises, so cooling pushes it up. HEPES moves half as much as Tris per degree, which is one reason it is preferred for work done on ice.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: You need a buffer at pH 8.20 from a weak acid whose pKa is 7.20. What ratio of conjugate base to acid does Henderson-Hasselbalch call for?
questions.explain: Each whole pH unit above the pKa multiplies the base-to-acid ratio by ten, because the relationship is logarithmic. Sitting one unit above the pKa also means the buffer is near the edge of its useful range.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: An acetate buffer has a pKa of 4.76. At pH 5.76, what fraction of the total buffer is in the acetate (conjugate base) form?
questions.explain: Turn the ratio into a fraction before answering: a 10 to 1 ratio is ten parts out of eleven, not ten percent. Half and half only happens when the pH equals the pKa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Glycine's residue mass is 57.05 Da and a water is 18.02 Da. What is the molecular weight of the tripeptide Gly-Gly-Gly?
questions.explain: A chain of n residues loses n-1 waters forming its peptide bonds, so you add exactly one water back for the two free ends, no matter how long the chain is. Summing free amino acid masses instead double counts two whole waters.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: The histidine side chain has a pKa of 6.0. What fraction of it is protonated at pH 7.0?
questions.explain: A base one full pH unit above its pKa is roughly one part in eleven protonated, which is why histidine is called basic but carries almost no charge in the cytosol. Half protonated would require the pH to equal the pKa.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: An enzyme has Vmax = 100 µM/min and Km = 25 µM. What is the initial velocity at [S] = 75 µM?
questions.explain: Three times Km does not mean three quarters of nothing: substituting into the hyperbola gives [S]/(Km+[S]) = 0.75 of Vmax. Reading Vmax straight off the plot is the usual error, since the curve only approaches it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A Lineweaver-Burk fit gives a y-intercept of 0.0100 and a slope of 0.250. What are Vmax and Km?
questions.explain: Take the reciprocal of the intercept first, then multiply the slope by that Vmax. Reading the slope as Km directly is the common slip, since the slope is really Km divided by Vmax.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A reaction has a standard free energy change of +15.0 kJ/mol. Coupled to ATP hydrolysis at -30.5 kJ/mol, what is the overall standard free energy change?
questions.explain: Free energies of coupled steps add, they do not multiply or cancel to the larger one's full value, so the uphill step is paid for and some driving force is left over. Flipping the sign of the hydrolysis term is the usual slip.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A researcher assays an enzyme with and without a new compound. Vmax is unchanged, but the apparent Km rises fourfold. The compound is most likely a:
questions.explain: Only one mechanism can leave the ceiling in place: if saturating substrate still reaches the same maximum rate, the inhibitor must be losing the race for the active site at high [S]. Anything that touches the enzyme-substrate complex drags Vmax down with it.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk plot, a student's inhibited line is steeper than the control but crosses the x-axis at exactly the same point. Which inhibitor was added?
questions.explain: The x-intercept is -1/Km, so a shared x-intercept means apparent Km never moved and the steeper slope must come from a smaller Vmax. Competitive inhibition is the one that shares the y-intercept instead, which is the single most common mix-up on this plot.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Adding a compound drops both apparent Km and apparent Vmax to one third of their control values, and the Lineweaver-Burk line stays parallel to the control. What kind of inhibition is this?
questions.explain: Parallel lines mean the slope Km/Vmax did not change, which only happens when Km and Vmax fall by the same factor. An inhibitor that can only bind the enzyme-substrate complex pulls substrate binding forward while capping turnover, so both numbers drop together.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: An inhibitor raises an enzyme's apparent Km and lowers its apparent Vmax at the same time, and the two Lineweaver-Burk lines meet above the x-axis rather than on either axis. What does that pattern indicate?
questions.explain: Km up and Vmax down at once cannot come from any of the three pure cases: competitive leaves Vmax alone, pure noncompetitive leaves Km alone, and uncompetitive lowers Km. It takes an inhibitor that binds free enzyme more tightly than the complex.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A protocol must hold pH 7.20 while the sample sits in a 4 C cold room, and you will titrate the buffer at the bench at 25 C. Which of these buffers holds the target best in the cold?
questions.explain: Matching the pKa to the target is only half the job: the temperature coefficient decides how far the buffer walks away once it is cold. Picking on pKa alone is what puts a cold room assay out of spec.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A short peptide has a free N terminus, a free C terminus and three basic side chains (two Lys, one Arg), and no acidic side chains. You load it onto an ion exchange column in a pH 8.0 buffer. What happens?
questions.explain: Work out the sign of the net charge at the running pH, then remember the resin is named for the ion it captures, not the charge it carries. Three basic groups against a single carboxylate leaves the peptide strongly positive well above pH 7, so it sticks to the negatively charged resin.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A student must find the pI of a peptide with a free C terminus (3.1), a free N terminus (9.0), one Lys (10.53) and one Arg (12.48). Which two pKa values should be averaged?
questions.explain: The right pair is the one that brackets the pH where the running net charge passes through zero, and with three bases against one acid that crossing sits at the top of the list, not in the middle. Reaching for the two middle values is the single most common way this calculation goes wrong.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A student computes the net charge of the dipeptide Asp-Tyr at pH 7.0. Counting the Asp side chain, the tyrosine hydroxyl and the C terminus as negative and the N terminus as positive, they report about -2. What is the real answer?
questions.explain: An acidic group is only negative once the pH climbs past its pKa, and tyrosine's phenol sits near 10, so at pH 7 it is still protonated and contributes nothing. Counting every acidic group as a full negative charge regardless of pH is what produces the extra unit.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Enzyme A has kcat = 100 per second and Km = 10 µM. Enzyme B has kcat = 1000 per second and Km = 500 µM. At the low substrate concentrations found in the cell, which enzyme processes substrate faster, and why?
choices: B, because its Vmax is larger
questions.explain: Below saturation the rate depends on how fast the enzyme captures substrate as well as how fast it turns it over, so the ratio of the two constants is what to compare. Turnover number alone only decides the winner when both enzymes are saturated.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: A cellular reaction has a standard free energy change of +4.0 kJ/mol at pH 7. The cell holds the reaction quotient Q at about 0.01 and runs at 37 C. Is the reaction spontaneous as it actually sits in the cell?
choices: No, the standard value is positive
Yes, but only above body heat
questions.explain: The standard value assumes every species at 1 M, which no cell does. Keeping products scarce makes Q small and the logarithm negative, which pulls the real free energy change down, often far enough to flip the sign.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.q: Lowering the salt concentration makes a purified enzyme fall apart into four identical pieces, and each piece still folds correctly and shows partial activity. Which level of structure was lost?
questions.explain: Separate polypeptide chains held together by noncovalent contacts are the only level that can come apart while each chain keeps its own fold and function. Losing the fold itself, or the sequence, would leave nothing active behind.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For a strong acid, [H⁺] equals:
questions.explain: Strong acids fully dissociate, so [H⁺] equals whatever concentration of acid you started with, no equilibrium calculation needed.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A buffer resists pH change best within about what range of its pKa?
questions.explain: Outside roughly pKa ± 1, one form of the buffer vastly outnumbers the other, leaving too little of the minority form to absorb added acid or base.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A reaction with negative ΔH and negative ΔS is spontaneous:
questions.explain: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With both ΔH and ΔS negative, low T keeps the favorable enthalpy term dominant; push T high enough and the entropy penalty takes over, flipping the reaction non-spontaneous.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At electrochemical equilibrium, the cell potential E equals:
questions.explain: At equilibrium Q = K and there is no net driving force left to push electrons, so E = 0, the same reason a fully discharged battery reads 0 V.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: At STP (0°C, 1 atm), one mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately:
questions.explain: This falls straight out of PV = nRT with n = 1, T = 273.15 K and P = 1 atm, so it is one case of the gas law rather than a separate rule to memorise.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In A = εbc, if the path length b doubles and everything else stays constant, absorbance A:
questions.explain: A is directly proportional to b, so the relationship is linear in path length, which is why a 0.5 cm cuvette halves the reading for the same sample.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A negative ΔG indicates a reaction is:
questions.explain: ΔG < 0 means the reaction releases free energy and proceeds as written under those conditions. Sign of ΔH alone does not decide it, since a heat-absorbing reaction can still run if ΔS is large enough.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solution at pH 3 has how many times more [H⁺] than one at pH 5?
questions.explain: pH is a base-10 log scale, so each whole unit is a tenfold change in [H⁺]. Two units apart is 10², not 2, which is the mistake of reading the scale as linear.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An absorbance of 0 corresponds to what percent transmittance?
questions.explain: Zero absorbance means nothing was absorbed, so all the light made it through. Reading 0 as 'no light' inverts the scale.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A concentration cell can produce nonzero voltage even with E° = 0 because:
choices: The electrodes are made of different metals
No current flows through the circuit
The temperature is held perfectly constant
questions.explain: The same electrode reaction on both sides forces E° = 0 by definition, but unequal concentrations make Q ≠ 1, and the −(RT/nF)lnQ term alone produces a real voltage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What does the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation relate?
choices: pH to pKa and the base/acid ratio
Ka to the ion product of water
questions.explain: pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When acid and conjugate base are equal the log term is zero, so pH equals pKa, which is also where buffering is strongest.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In C1V1 = C2V2, what is being held constant?
questions.explain: Dilution adds solvent without adding solute, so the amount of solute is unchanged. That conservation is the entire basis of the equation, and it is why volume and concentration both move.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A solution goes from pH 5 to pH 3. The hydrogen ion concentration changes how?
questions.explain: pH is a base-10 logarithm, so each unit is a tenfold change, and a falling pH means rising acidity. Reading the drop as a decrease in [H⁺] gets the direction backwards.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In Beer-Lambert, absorbance is proportional to which pair?
questions.explain: A = ε × b × c. Wavelength fixes ε rather than entering the product, and temperature does not appear at all, so neither belongs in the pair.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What does a very large equilibrium constant K tell you?
questions.explain: K describes position, not speed. A reaction can have an enormous K and still be immeasurably slow without a catalyst, which is exactly why enzymes are necessary.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Which reagent determines how much product a reaction can make?
questions.explain: Whichever reactant runs out first caps the yield, and it is found by comparing moles divided by coefficient, never by raw mass. Everything else is left over in excess.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In PV = nRT, what happens to volume if temperature doubles at fixed pressure?
questions.explain: At fixed pressure and amount, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature. The temperature must be in kelvin, since doubling 20°C is not doubling T.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Molarity is defined as what?
choices: Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
Moles of solute per litre of solution
Moles of solute per litre of solvent
Grams of solute per litre of solution
questions.explain: It is per litre of final solution, not of solvent. Dissolving solute changes the total volume, which is why you top the flask up to the mark instead of adding a litre of water.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Percent yield compares which two quantities?
questions.explain: Actual divided by theoretical, times 100. Flipping the ratio turns every normal result into a number above 100, which is the giveaway that the division went the wrong way.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A rigid 0.500 L vessel holds 2.00 mol of gas at 300 K. What is the pressure in atm?
questions.explain: Rearrange PV = nRT to P = nRT/V. Dividing by the volume is the step people drop, which leaves the answer short by exactly the factor V.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: What is the pH of a 0.010 M strong base solution at 25°C?
questions.explain: A strong base gives [OH⁻] equal to its concentration, so you find pOH first and then subtract from 14. Taking the log of the concentration straight away gives the pOH, not the pH.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sample reads A = 0.90 in a 1 cm cuvette, and ε = 4500 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. What is the concentration?
questions.explain: Rearrange A = εbc to c = A/(εb). With b = 1 cm the path length drops out, so the only arithmetic left is one division.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A first-order reaction has k = 0.0693 s⁻¹. What is its half-life?
questions.explain: For first order the half-life is ln2/k and carries no concentration term, which is why each successive half-life takes the same time.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In water, H₂O, what percent of the mass is oxygen? (H = 1.008, O = 15.999)
questions.explain: Mass percent weights each element by its atomic mass, not its atom count. Two hydrogens outnumber the one oxygen but weigh about a sixteenth as much each.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For 2 Al + 3 Cl₂ → 2 AlCl₃ you have 0.400 mol Al and 0.450 mol Cl₂. Which is limiting?
questions.explain: Compare moles divided by coefficient, since reactants are consumed in the coefficient ratio. The reactant with more moles can still run out first.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 25.0 g and you recover 20.0 g. What is the percent yield?
questions.explain: Actual over theoretical, times 100. Dividing the other way gives a number above 100, which is impossible for a genuine yield.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A cell has E° = 0.400 V, n = 1 and Q = 0.00100 at 25°C. What is E?
questions.explain: The Nernst correction subtracts (0.0592/n)logQ at 25°C, so a Q below 1 makes the log negative and pushes E above E°. Dropping the minus sign moves the answer the wrong way.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For A ⇌ B + C with [A]₀ = 1.00 M and Keq = 0.100, what is x at equilibrium?
questions.explain: Keq = x²/([A]₀ − x) is a quadratic, so solve it rather than assuming the denominator is still [A]₀. Here the shortcut √(Keq·[A]₀) is off by a sixth, because x is not small next to 1.00 M.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A student weighs 6.2 g of product where stoichiometry predicts 8.0 g, then discovers the balance has been reading 0.3 g high all day. What is the corrected percent yield?
questions.explain: The offset is on the measured mass, so subtract it from the recovered amount before dividing. Correcting the theoretical value instead, or adding rather than subtracting, both move the answer up when it should come down.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A technician fills a rigid 2.00 L cylinder with 0.500 mol of gas and records the temperature as 27°C. What pressure should the gauge read?
questions.explain: PV = nRT only holds with temperature measured from absolute zero, so convert to kelvin by adding 273.15 before dividing by the volume. Using the Celsius number, or rounding the conversion to 273, both shift the result.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: An exothermic gas synthesis sits at equilibrium. A technician raises the temperature to speed it up and is surprised the product yield falls. What explains it?
choices: Heat behaves as a product, so adding it shifts the system left
Higher temperature always slows down the forward reaction step
The higher temperature destroys the catalyst and halts the reaction
Raising the temperature lowers Keq for every reaction, either way
questions.explain: Temperature is the one stress that changes Keq itself, and for a heat-releasing reaction more heat pushes the balance back toward reactants. The rate does rise, which is why the yield drop surprises people.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A student measures pH 1.00 for 0.10 M hydrochloric acid and assumes 0.10 M acetic acid (pKa 4.76) will read the same. What pH does the acetic acid actually give?
questions.explain: A weak acid only partly dissociates, so [H⁺] is far below the total acid concentration and you must solve the equilibrium. Quoting the pKa, or forgetting to halve in the shortcut, both land far from the real reading.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A cell with E° = 0.80 V and n = 1 runs at 25°C until products build up to Q = 1000. A student reports E = 0.98 V. What is E actually?
questions.explain: Products accumulating raise Q above 1, the log goes positive, and the Nernst term is subtracted, so the potential must fall below E°. Reporting a rise means the sign of the correction was flipped.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A drug level falls from 80 mg/L to 40 mg/L in 3 hours, then from 40 mg/L to 20 mg/L over the next 3 hours. Starting at 80 mg/L, how long until it reaches 5 mg/L?
questions.explain: A half-life that stays the same across successive halvings is the signature of first order, so you can simply count halvings. Stopping at 10 mg/L is the usual slip, since that is only three of them.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A sample reads A = 0.45 in a 0.50 cm cuvette with ε = 6000 M⁻¹cm⁻¹. A student assumes the usual 1 cm path. What is the true concentration?
questions.explain: Path length sits in the denominator of c = A/(εb), so a shorter cuvette means the real concentration is higher than the 1 cm assumption suggests. Multiplying by 0.50 instead of dividing moves it the wrong way.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A compound is 82.7% carbon and 17.3% hydrogen by mass, with a molar mass of 58.12 g/mol. A student reports the simplest ratio as the answer. What is the molecular formula?
questions.explain: The simplest ratio only fixes proportions, so you must divide the real molar mass by the empirical formula mass and scale every subscript. Rounding a 2.49 ratio down to 2 instead of clearing the half also breaks the formula.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: 28 g of N₂ (28.014 g/mol) reacts with 10 g of H₂ (2.016 g/mol) in N₂ + 3 H₂ → 2 NH₃, and 30 g of ammonia is recovered. A student calls H₂ limiting because 10 g is the smaller mass. What is the real percent yield?
questions.explain: Mass never identifies the limiting reactant, moles divided by coefficient does, and here the lighter reagent is in excess. Carrying the wrong limiting reagent inflates the theoretical yield and so deflates the percentage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A reaction has ΔH = −40 kJ/mol and ΔS = −100 J/mol·K. A chemist running it at 450 K cannot get it to proceed. Above what temperature does it stop being spontaneous?
questions.explain: The crossover sits at T = ΔH/ΔS, and the two must share units, so convert the entropy from joules to kilojoules first. Leaving it in joules shrinks the answer by a factor of a thousand.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: A technician finds Q = 4 in a vessel whose Keq is 25 and concludes there is too much product. What is actually true of the system?
choices: Q sits below K, so the reaction runs forward
Q sits above K, so the reaction must run backward
Q already equals K, so the system is fully at rest
Q and K cannot be compared within a single vessel
questions.explain: Q and K use the same expression at different moments, so the comparison alone gives the direction: a Q under K means products are still too scarce. Adding more product here would push the system further from balance.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Crossing Aa × Aa (one gene, complete dominance) gives what phenotype ratio?
questions.explain: 3 out of 4 offspring show the dominant phenotype (AA, Aa, Aa), 1 shows recessive (aa). The 1:2:1 trap is the genotype ratio, not the phenotype ratio.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Under Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium with q = 0.3, what fraction of the population is heterozygous?
questions.explain: Heterozygote frequency is the 2pq term. The 0.09 trap is q squared, the recessive homozygotes, and 0.49 is p squared.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A test cross breeds an unknown-genotype individual with:
questions.explain: Only a recessive partner contributes nothing dominant, so every offspring phenotype reads the unknown parent's gametes directly. All-dominant offspring means AA, a roughly 1:1 split means Aa.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the five Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium assumptions?
choices: No new mutation at the locus
questions.explain: Equilibrium requires that nothing changes allele frequencies, so the model assumes selection is absent. Active selection is one of the forces that pushes a population off the p squared, 2pq, q squared curve.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Two type A parents have a type O child. Is that possible?
questions.explain: A blood test reports the phenotype, which cannot tell AA from AO. Reading a phenotype as if it were the genotype is the error behind most paternity confusion.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An AB parent and an O parent can have which blood types of child?
questions.explain: The AB parent always passes A or B and the O parent always passes O, so every child is AO or BO. This is the one cross where neither parent's own type can appear in the child.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In Hardy-Weinberg, what does 2pq represent?
questions.explain: The factor of two is there because a heterozygote can be assembled two ways, a dominant egg with a recessive sperm or the reverse. Dropping it is the single most common Hardy-Weinberg slip.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: If q equals 0.1 for a recessive allele, what fraction of the population are carriers?
questions.explain: Carriers are the heterozygotes, so this is the 2pq term. Note that carriers outnumber affected individuals eighteen to one here, which is why rare recessive alleles persist.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Why are X-linked recessive conditions more common in males?
questions.explain: With a single X there is no second copy to mask a recessive allele, so one hit is enough. A female needs the allele on both X chromosomes, which is far rarer.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid cross AaBb x AaBb gives which phenotype ratio?
questions.explain: That ratio assumes the two genes assort independently. Linked genes on the same chromosome distort it toward the parental combinations, which is how linkage was discovered.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: What does a chi-square goodness of fit test compare?
choices: Two allele frequencies to each other
A genotype ratio to a phenotype ratio
One generation's counts to the next
questions.explain: The test asks whether a deviation from a predicted ratio is bigger than sampling noise. It needs raw counts, not percentages, because the sample size is what decides whether a gap matters.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Which genotypes give an Rh positive phenotype?
questions.explain: D is dominant, so one copy is enough to put the antigen on the red cell. That is why two Rh positive parents can still have an Rh negative child, if both are carriers.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A recessive disorder affects 1 in 400 people. Under Hardy-Weinberg, what fraction of the population are carriers?
questions.explain: Affected people are the q squared class, so take a square root first to get the allele frequency, then build the heterozygote term. Answering 0.05 stops at the allele frequency instead of the carrier frequency.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 500 is genotyped as 320 AA, 160 Aa and 20 aa. What is the frequency of the A allele?
questions.explain: Count alleles, not people: every homozygote contributes two copies and every heterozygote one. Answering 0.64 reports the AA genotype frequency, which is p squared rather than p.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: Counting 180 AA, 120 Aa and 100 aa individuals, what is q by direct allele counting?
questions.explain: Direct counting needs no equilibrium assumption, which is the point of doing it when all three genotypes are visible. The 0.50 trap is the square root of aa over N, a shortcut that is only valid at equilibrium.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In an AaBb x AaBb dihybrid cross, what fraction of the 16 boxes are aabb?
questions.explain: Each parent makes an ab gamete one time in four, and the two events are independent, so multiply the two quarters. Answering 1/4 multiplies nothing and treats the two genes as one.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A type AB parent and a type O parent. What percent of their children are expected to be type A?
questions.explain: The O parent can only pass O, so the child's type is decided entirely by which allele the AB parent sends. Half the children get A and half get B, and no child is AB or O.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An AO parent and a BO parent. What is the chance of a type O child?
questions.explain: Only the box where both parents happen to send their O allele gives OO, and each sends O half the time. This is the cross where all four blood types are possible from one pairing.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A carrier mother and an unaffected father, X-linked recessive trait. What fraction of all their children are expected to be affected?
questions.explain: Half the sons are affected, but sons are only half the children, so the two halves multiply. Answering 50 percent quotes the risk within the sons and forgets to scale it to all children.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A monohybrid cross gives 84 tall and 36 short plants. Tested against 3:1, what is the chi-square value?
questions.explain: Work out each expected count from the total first, then add one squared-difference term per class. The 3.84 trap is the critical value you compare against, not the statistic itself.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A pediatrician delivers a type O newborn. The mother is type A and the listed father is type AB, and he disputes paternity. What does the blood typing establish?
choices: AB passes A or B, so this man is excluded
He could still be the father if he is AO
Blood type can never exclude a father here
The typing proves he is the father
questions.explain: An AB individual has no O allele to give, so every child of his carries A or B and shows it. Exclusion is the only thing ABO typing can do well: it never confirms paternity, because millions of men share any blood type.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: An Rh negative mother and an Rh positive father have an Rh positive first child. What can you say about the second child?
choices: The second child must also be Rh positive
The chance drops because one was positive
The father must be DD, so every child is positive
The chance of Rh positive is 50 to 100 percent
questions.explain: Rh positive covers both DD and Dd, and the first child being positive does not tell you which the father is, so the honest answer is a range. Each conception is independent, so no earlier child shifts the odds.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 500 has 400 AA, 50 Aa and 50 aa. A student takes the square root of 50/500 and reports q = 0.32, but counting alleles gives q = 0.15. Why do they disagree?
choices: The student should have used the 2pq term instead
Counting only works on very large samples
The square root shortcut assumes equilibrium
Both are right, they just round differently
questions.explain: Taking the root of the recessive frequency only recovers q when the genotypes already sit on the p squared, 2pq, q squared curve. Here they do not, so counting alleles is the answer and the gap between the two numbers is the evidence.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A tall plant of unknown genotype is crossed with a short plant. The 50 offspring are 28 tall and 22 short, and chi-square against 1:1 is 0.72 with df 1. What does this support?
choices: The tall parent was homozygous dominant
The data reject Mendelian inheritance here
The cross was really a 3:1 monohybrid
questions.explain: A homozygous dominant parent crossed to a recessive gives no short offspring at all, so 22 of them rules it out immediately. A chi-square of 0.72 is well under the 3.84 cutoff, so the 28 to 22 wobble is just sampling noise.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid cross gives 99, 27, 27 and 7 offspring in the four classes. Chi-square against 9:3:3:1 is 2.40. What is the right conclusion?
choices: The df is 4, so the test cannot be read
questions.explain: Degrees of freedom are one fewer than the number of classes, so df is 3 and the cutoff is 7.81. Failing to reject a ratio is not the same as proving it, since the test can only ever say the data are compatible.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A colorblind man and a woman with normal vision and no family history of colorblindness have a colorblind son. Where did the son's allele come from?
choices: From his mother, who is a carrier
From a brand new mutation in his father
questions.explain: A son takes his Y from his father and his only X from his mother, so a father can never pass an X-linked allele to a son. No family history just means the carrier mothers before her happened to have no affected sons.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A type O baby is born to a type A mother and a type B father, and the ward suspects a sample mix-up. What is the right conclusion?
choices: A type A and type B couple cannot do this at all
Both parents carry O, so 1 in 4 is type O
The baby must carry a new mutation
One parent is really type AB, not A or B
questions.explain: A and B are each dominant over O, so an AO parent and a BO parent look like plain A and B while both still carry a hidden O. This is the one parental pairing that can produce all four blood types.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A population of 200 has 90 AA, 20 Aa and 90 aa. Chi-square against Hardy-Weinberg is 128 with df 1. What does that let you say?
choices: Natural selection is acting on this locus
The allele frequencies were computed wrong
It returns to equilibrium next generation
At least one assumption is being violated
questions.explain: The test only detects that the genotypes are off the predicted curve, never which of the five assumptions failed. A heterozygote shortfall this large usually points at non-random mating or two subpopulations sampled as one.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: A dihybrid test cross AaBb x aabb should give 1:1:1:1, but 100 offspring come out 45, 5, 5 and 45. Chi-square is 64 with df 3. What explains it?
choices: One of the two genes is X-linked
The two genes sit on one chromosome
A sample of 100 offspring is too small
questions.explain: The excess sits in the two parental combinations and the shortfall in the two recombinants, which is the signature of genes travelling together. A larger sample would only make the deviation more significant, not less.

questions.subject: Genetics
questions.q: In a sample of 100 people, 84 show the dominant phenotype and 16 the recessive. A student reports p = 0.84. What is p actually?
questions.explain: The 84 percent lumps homozygous dominants together with heterozygotes, so it is p squared plus 2pq, not p. Start from the recessive class instead, because that is the only group whose genotype the phenotype reveals.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Textbooks give 30, 32, 36 or 38 ATP for one glucose's total aerobic yield. That disagreement comes from two different values used for:
questions.explain: Older courses use 3 ATP per NADH and 2 per FADH2, which lands on 36 or 38. Modern measured values of 2.5 and 1.5 land on 30 or 32, and the shuttle then picks between each pair.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: One full turn of the citric acid cycle (per acetyl-CoA) produces how many NADH?
questions.explain: Three steps make it: isocitrate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase and malate dehydrogenase. People guess 4 by counting succinate dehydrogenase, but that step makes FADH2 instead.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Where in the cell does glycolysis take place?
questions.explain: All ten steps run outside the mitochondrion, which is why a mature red blood cell with no mitochondria at all can still break down glucose for energy.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Which molecule directly links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle?
questions.explain: Pyruvate is where glycolysis stops, but the cycle cannot accept it until pyruvate dehydrogenase strips a carbon off as CO2. That decarboxylation is irreversible, which is why fat can never become glucose.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: How much ATP or GTP is made directly in one turn of the citric acid cycle?
questions.explain: Only succinyl-CoA synthetase phosphorylates anything at the substrate level. The old figure of 12 counts the NADH and FADH2 as if they were already ATP, which they are not until the chain cashes them in.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Which citric acid cycle enzyme is also part of the electron transport chain?
questions.explain: It is Complex II, bolted into the inner membrane. Every other cycle enzyme floats free in the matrix and hands its electrons to a soluble carrier rather than straight into the chain.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Complete oxidation of one glucose yields roughly how much ATP by modern counts?
questions.explain: The modern range comes from measured P/O ratios of 2.5 and 1.5 instead of the older whole numbers. The 36 to 38 figure is not wrong, it is just the older convention, so always say which one you are using.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: How many nitrogen atoms does one turn of the urea cycle dispose of?
questions.explain: One arrives as free ammonia at step 1 and the second comes from aspartate at step 3. The aspartate nitrogen is the one most people miss, because it looks like a carbon donor.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Glycolysis nets how much ATP when no oxygen is available?
questions.explain: No step in the pathway touches oxygen, so the yield cannot change. What changes is downstream: pyruvate becomes lactate or ethanol purely to hand NAD+ back, or the pathway stalls at step 6.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Beta oxidation of a fatty acid produces which pair per round?
questions.explain: Each round shortens the chain by two carbons and also releases one acetyl-CoA. No ATP is made in the round itself, so the whole yield arrives later through the chain and the cycle.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: The 2 CO2 released per turn of the citric acid cycle come from where?
questions.explain: Isocitrate dehydrogenase releases the first carbon and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase the second, each while reducing NAD+. The chain releases no carbon at all, it only reduces oxygen to water.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Which citric acid cycle enzyme catalyzes the committed, regulated condensation that opens the turn?
questions.explain: It joins the two-carbon acetyl group to four-carbon oxaloacetate, so once it fires the carbon is in the cycle. Isocitrate dehydrogenase is also regulated, but it is the rate limiting step, not the committing one.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Why is the urea cycle usually costed at 4 ATP-equivalents rather than 3?
choices: The cycle has to run twice
questions.explain: Carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I spends 2 ATP outright. Argininosuccinate synthetase spends only one ATP but breaks two high-energy bonds doing it, so it is counted as 2 rather than 1.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A liver cell uses the malate-aspartate shuttle. On modern P/O ratios of 2.5 and 1.5, what is its total ATP per glucose?
questions.explain: The shuttle decides what the 2 cytosolic NADH are worth, and malate-aspartate delivers them at full NADH value. Students who answer 38 have used the classic ratios by mistake.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Classic P/O ratios of 3.0 and 2.0 with the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle give what total per glucose?
questions.explain: Classic ratios on their own give 38. The glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle then downgrades the 2 cytosolic NADH to FADH2 value, costing 2 ATP, which is why 38 is the trap here.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Of the ATP made per glucose, how much comes from substrate-level phosphorylation rather than from the chain?
questions.explain: Glycolysis hands over 2 and the cycle's GTP hands over 2 more, since the cycle turns twice per glucose. Answering 2 counts only glycolysis and forgets succinyl-CoA synthetase.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: The ATP yield page counts 10 NADH per glucose. How many of those 10 are made inside the mitochondrion?
questions.explain: Only glycolysis makes NADH outside, and it makes 2. The rest come from pyruvate dehydrogenase and the cycle, which is why only 2 of the 10 ever need a shuttle.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Palmitate has 16 carbons. How many rounds of beta oxidation does breaking it down completely take?
questions.explain: The count is n/2 minus 1, not n/2, because the last round splits a four-carbon piece into two acetyl-CoA at once. Answering 8 is the classic off-by-one here.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A 12-carbon saturated fatty acid is fully oxidized. How many acetyl-CoA, and how many rounds of beta oxidation?
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA count is n/2 and the round count is one fewer, so the two numbers never match. A 12 in the first slot comes from counting carbons rather than two-carbon units.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A 12-carbon fatty acid gives 23 NADH, 11 FADH2 and 6 GTP. On modern ratios, with activation paid, what is its total?
questions.explain: Take 23 at 2.5 and 11 at 1.5, add the GTP, then subtract the 2 ATP activation cost that is paid once per fatty acid no matter its length. Skipping that subtraction gives 80.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A liver disposes of 10 nitrogen atoms as urea. How many ATP-equivalents does that cost, and how many urea form?
questions.explain: Each turn buries 2 nitrogen atoms in 1 urea for 4 ATP-equivalents, so 10 nitrogens is 5 turns. Answering 10 urea treats one nitrogen per molecule, but urea carries two.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: One glucose sends 2 acetyl-CoA through the citric acid cycle. What does that come to in total?
questions.explain: Per turn the cycle gives 3 NADH, 1 FADH2 and 1 GTP, and one glucose makes two acetyl-CoA, so double everything. The 8 NADH figure belongs to the whole glucose, pyruvate dehydrogenase included.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Glycolysis makes 2 ATP at step 7 and 2 at step 10, and spends 1 each at steps 1 and 3. What are the gross and the net?
questions.explain: Four are made and two were already spent priming the sugar, so the cell finishes two ahead. A question asking what the cell gains wants the net, which is where the 4 answer loses marks.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Leucine, valine and isoleucine are the three branched-chain amino acids. Which classification does each one get?
choices: Leu keto, Val gluco, Ile both
Leu both, Val keto, Ile gluco
questions.explain: Branched-chain does not mean one category. Valine's skeleton lands on succinyl-CoA so it can make glucose, while isoleucine splits into two skeletons and counts as both.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A muscle cell switches to anaerobic conditions mid-contraction. Per glucose, what is its ATP yield now?
questions.explain: Only glycolysis keeps paying, and it pays net, not gross: 4 made minus 2 invested. The cycle's 2 GTP go too, because the cycle stalls once NAD+ stops coming back from the chain.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A student reasons that anaerobic yield is the 30 ATP total minus the chain's 26, leaving 4. Where does that break?
choices: The chain actually gives 28 of the 30 ATP
Glycolysis nets 4 ATP, so 4 is right
The cycle's 2 GTP stop without the chain
questions.explain: Subtracting the chain leaves the 4 substrate-level ATP on paper, but 2 of those are the cycle's GTP, and the cycle cannot turn without NAD+ coming back. Only glycolysis is genuinely oxygen independent.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A muscle cell on the glycerol-3-phosphate shuttle totals 30 ATP per glucose. How much of that 30 does glycolysis itself account for?
questions.explain: Glycolysis pays twice: directly, and again through the 2 NADH it hands to the shuttle. Answering 2 counts only the substrate-level ATP and ignores what those cytosolic NADH are worth.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: The same glucose yields 32 ATP in a liver cell and 30 in a muscle cell on identical P/O ratios. What accounts for the gap?
choices: Liver's shuttle delivers its 2 NADH at full value
Liver makes two extra GTP in the cycle per glucose
Muscle runs the cycle once rather than twice
Muscle spends 2 ATP making lactate instead
questions.explain: The NADH is identical in both cells, but it cannot cross the inner membrane, so the tissue's shuttle decides whether its electrons arrive worth 2.5 or 1.5 ATP each. Two NADH at a 1 ATP difference is the whole 2 ATP gap.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Cyanide blocks complex IV in a cell oxidizing glucose. Why does the citric acid cycle stop, when none of its own enzymes are inhibited?
choices: Complex IV is the source of the cycle's GTP
NAD+ is no longer regenerated for it
The cycle's own enzymes need oxygen directly
Oxaloacetate gets consumed by complex IV
questions.explain: Three of the eight steps need NAD+ as the electron acceptor, and the only thing that strips electrons back off NADH is the chain. Block the chain and the cycle runs out of acceptor, not out of enzyme.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A patient on a long fast is making glucose from amino acids. Why can leucine and lysine contribute none of it?
choices: Both are essential, so the body cannot use them
Their nitrogen is locked into urea beforehand
They are burned in the cycle before entry
questions.explain: Their skeletons land on acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA, and there is no human enzyme that walks acetyl-CoA back up to pyruvate. Those carbons can still be burned for energy, they just cannot become sugar.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A newborn has high blood ammonia, yet every urea cycle enzyme assays normal. Which defect fits that picture?
choices: Arginase is missing from the cytosol
questions.explain: The cycle needs an activator as well as enzymes: without N-acetylglutamate, CPS1 will not fire even though it is present and intact. Picking a missing enzyme contradicts the normal assays in the stem.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: After days of fasting a liver is flooded with acetyl-CoA from beta oxidation, but exports ketone bodies instead of burning it all. Why?
choices: Oxaloacetate has been pulled into gluconeogenesis
Acetyl-CoA cannot cross into the matrix when fasting
Beta oxidation stops producing any NADH by then
The cycle's enzymes are switched off while fasting
questions.explain: Acetyl-CoA can only enter the cycle by condensing with oxaloacetate, and fasting spends that oxaloacetate making glucose instead. The cycle is not switched off, it is short of its partner.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: Palmitate gives 106 ATP from 16 carbons and glucose 32 from 6. A student says fat is 3.3 times better per carbon. Fix it.
choices: About 2 times, as stored per gram
questions.explain: Dividing 106 by 32 compares whole molecules, not carbons, and palmitate brings nearly three times as many carbons to the comparison. Divide each total by its own carbon count first.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A student computes a 14-carbon fatty acid at 94 ATP on modern ratios, but the calculator gives 92. What was most likely forgotten?
choices: One of the six beta oxidation rounds
The 7 GTP from the seven cycle turns
That FADH2 is worth 1.5 and not 2.5
questions.explain: Every other term checks out at 94, so the missing 2 is the one-off charge for attaching coenzyme A before any of this starts. Dropping a round or a GTP would be off by much more than 2.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A cell with plenty of ATP and citrate slows glucose breakdown. Which glycolytic step is the brake, and why is it not step 1?
choices: Hexokinase, the first ATP spent here
Pyruvate kinase, the final step of ten
PFK-1, since G6P has other fates
questions.explain: Step 1 only traps the sugar as glucose-6-phosphate, which can still go to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway. The first step committed to glycolysis alone is the one worth regulating.

questions.subject: Metabolism
questions.q: A mature red blood cell has no mitochondria. Per glucose, what does it get, and what must it do with its NADH?
questions.explain: With no mitochondrion there is no chain and no cycle, so the cell lives on the net from glycolysis and has to dump its electrons onto pyruvate to get NAD+ back. A shuttle needs a mitochondrion to shuttle into.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: What is the net ATP yield of glycolysis per glucose molecule?
questions.explain: 4 ATP are produced in the payoff phase, but 2 were invested early on, net 2 ATP, plus 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Which mRNA codon signals the start of translation?
questions.explain: AUG codes for methionine and is recognized by the initiator tRNA to begin translation, the other three are stop codons.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Which of these is NOT a stop codon?
questions.explain: UAA, UAG and UGA all signal stop. AUG codes for methionine and doubles as the start codon.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Which factor increases a DNA primer's melting temperature (Tm)?
questions.explain: A G to C pair holds three hydrogen bonds against two for A to T, so more energy is needed to pull the strands apart. Shortening the primer or dropping the salt both push Tm down, not up.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the committed, rate-limiting step of glycolysis?
questions.explain: This is the first irreversible step unique to glycolysis. Hexokinase comes earlier but its product can still be routed to glycogen or the pentose phosphate pathway, so it is not the commitment point.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Which amino acid does the start codon AUG specify?
questions.explain: The start codon is not a separate signal bolted onto the code, it is a normal codon that also recruits the initiator tRNA. In bacteria that first residue is formylated, but the codon is unchanged.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides in which direction?
questions.explain: The enzyme needs a free 3' hydroxyl to attack the incoming nucleotide, so the template never changes the direction. That one constraint is why the lagging strand has to be built in Okazaki fragments.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A 260/280 ratio near 1.8 suggests what?
questions.explain: About 1.8 is the usual target for DNA and about 2.0 for RNA. Protein and phenol both absorb at 280 nm, so they pull the ratio down rather than leaving it at target.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: The genetic code is described as degenerate because what?
choices: The code is read in overlapping triplets
Several codons can mean one amino acid
A codon can mean two amino acids
Three codons specify nothing at all
questions.explain: 61 coding codons have to cover 20 amino acids, so most amino acids get more than one. Degeneracy sits mostly in the third base, which is why third position changes are often silent. The three stop codons are a separate fact, not what degenerate means.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Translating a DNA coding strand to protein, what replaces thymine?
questions.explain: RNA carries this base in place of thymine. The mRNA otherwise matches the coding strand, which is why you can read protein straight off it once you know the frame.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: How many codons specify amino acids, out of 64 total?
questions.explain: Three of the 64 are stop codons, so they come off the total. Answering 20 confuses the number of amino acids with the number of codons that encode them.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A dsDNA sample was diluted 1:20 before reading, and the A260 comes back 0.300. What is the concentration of the undiluted stock?
questions.explain: The A260 describes what is in the cuvette, so the dilution factor multiplies back up to the stock. Leaving it out is the most common slip here and costs you a factor of 20.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: An RNA sample was diluted 1:100 and reads A260 = 0.250. What is the stock concentration?
questions.explain: RNA converts at a different factor from DNA because its bases are more exposed and absorb more per microgram. Reaching for 50 is a DNA habit and reads 25 percent high.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: An oligo (single-stranded DNA) is read undiluted and gives A260 = 0.600. What is its concentration?
questions.explain: Single-stranded DNA takes the lowest of the three factors, so the same absorbance means less material than it would for duplex DNA. Using the dsDNA number here overstates an oligo stock by about half.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A 10-base oligo contains 4 G or C bases and 6 A or T bases. What is its Tm by the Wallace rule?
questions.explain: The rule weights each GC pair at 4 degrees and each AT pair at 2, because the GC pair holds one more hydrogen bond. Swapping the two coefficients is the usual arithmetic error.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A 24-base primer contains 6 G and 9 C. What is its GC content?
questions.explain: GC content is the G and C count over the full length, so both bases are counted together. 37.5 percent is the AT content, the complement of the right answer rather than the answer.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A 30-base primer has 15 G or C bases. What is its Tm by the long-sequence formula on this page?
questions.explain: Above 14 bases the Wallace rule runs far too hot, which is why the page switches formulas by length. Note that the GC term is subtracted here, since 15 sits below the 16.4 constant.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: An open reading frame is 300 nucleotides long, counting its stop codon. How many amino acids are in the finished protein?
questions.explain: Divide by three to get codons, then drop the stop codon, which carries no amino acid of its own. Answering 100 counts the stop as a residue.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Reading the DNA coding strand ATGCATTGG in frame 1, which peptide do you get?
questions.explain: Transcribe by swapping T for U, then cut into threes before looking anything up. Most errors here come from misreading the third base of the middle codon, which is where the code is most degenerate.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A coding strand reads 5'-ATGCCGTTAC-3'. What is its reverse complement?
questions.explain: Two steps have to both happen: pair every base, then read the new strand back to front. Complementing without reversing is the single most common mistake when designing a reverse primer.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A DNA prep reads A260 = 0.360 and A280 = 0.200. What is the 260/280 ratio, and how does the calculator read it?
questions.explain: The ratio is A260 over A280, in that order, and 1.8 is the DNA target rather than a warning. Dividing the other way gives a number below 1 that cannot be compared to any of the published bands.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: An RNA prep reads 260/280 of 2.05 and 260/230 of 1.2. It looks clean by one measure and not the other. What is the most likely contaminant, and what does it do downstream?
choices: Protein carryover, which the low 260/230 is reporting
Nothing, because 2.05 already reads as clean
Guanidine or phenol, which inhibits the RT step
Genomic DNA, flagged by the 260/280 reading
questions.explain: The two ratios watch different windows, so a prep can pass one and fail the other. Protein shows up at 280 nm, not 230, and a ratio that passes one check never clears the prep on its own.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A dsDNA sample is diluted 1:50 and reads A260 = 0.400. The student writes down 20 ng/uL. What went wrong, and what is the real stock concentration?
choices: The RNA factor was used, so it is 800 ng/uL
Nothing went wrong, 20 ng/uL is the stock value
The dilution was divided in, so it is 0.4 ng/uL
The dilution was left out, so it is 1000 ng/uL
questions.explain: The reading belongs to the cuvette, not the tube on ice, so the dilution factor multiplies rather than divides. 20 is exactly the cuvette concentration, which is why the mistake looks like a plausible answer.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Two 20-base primers go into the same PCR, one at 60 percent GC and one at 40 percent GC. The reaction gives faint product plus extra bands. Using the long-sequence formula, what explains it?
choices: Their Tm values sit about 8 C apart, 56 and 48
Both are 20 bases, so their Tm values match
The GC-rich primer is the weaker binder here
GC content moves the yield only, never the Tm value
questions.explain: One annealing temperature has to serve both primers, so a gap this wide leaves one primer binding loosely and seeding mispriming. Equal length does not mean equal Tm, because the formula is driven by the GC count.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A point mutation changes an mRNA codon from GAA to GAG. What is the consequence for the protein?
choices: Glutamate is replaced by aspartate there
None, since both codons call for glutamate
The chain stops early at that codon instead
Every codon after it shifts out of register
questions.explain: Third position changes often land on a synonym, which is where the code's degeneracy lives. A frameshift needs a base added or lost, not swapped, so a one for one substitution never shifts the frame.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A single base change turns the codon UAU into UAA partway through a transcript. What happens to the protein?
choices: Tyrosine is swapped for another aromatic residue
Nothing, third position changes are silent
Translation ends there, giving a short chain
The reading frame shifts from that point on
questions.explain: This is the case where a third position change is not harmless, because it lands on a stop rather than a synonym. Treating all third position changes as silent is the trap, and the chain is truncated, not merely altered.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: One extra base is inserted just after the start codon of an mRNA. What does the ribosome produce?
choices: The same protein with one extra residue added
The same protein, since the code is degenerate
A protein changed only where the base was inserted
A garbled chain that usually hits an early stop
questions.explain: Codons are read in non-overlapping threes, so one extra base regroups every base downstream into different codons. The damage is not local, and a stop codon usually turns up by chance within a few dozen codons.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: E. coli is grown with both glucose and lactose present. What does the lac operon do, and why?
choices: Basal transcription only, since CAP is inactive
Maximum transcription, since lactose is available
Fully off, since glucose blocks the operator
Fully off, since the repressor cannot come off
questions.explain: Two switches have to agree: lactose takes the repressor off the operator, and low glucose raises cAMP so CAP can help polymerase bind. Glucose never touches the operator, it works through cAMP, so the operon is leaky rather than shut.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A mutant trp repressor still binds the operator but can no longer bind tryptophan. What is the phenotype?
choices: The operon stays off whatever the tryptophan level
The operon stays on even with tryptophan around
The operon now needs an inducer, the way lac does
No change, since trp control is positive control
questions.explain: Tryptophan is a corepressor: it has to bind the repressor to switch the operon off, so a repressor deaf to it can never be activated. The cell keeps making tryptophan it does not need, which is the mirror image of a lac repressor mutant.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: A cya mutant that cannot make cAMP is grown with lactose and no glucose. What does the lac operon do?
choices: Only basal transcription, because CAP cannot form
Maximum transcription, because the lactose is there
Nothing at all, because the repressor stays bound
Maximum transcription, because glucose is absent
questions.explain: Positive control runs through CAP bound to cAMP, so no cAMP means no CAP no matter how low glucose is. The repressor is still off the operator, which is why some transcription happens rather than none.

questions.subject: Molecular biology
questions.q: Deleting a sequence 10 kb upstream of a human gene cuts expression twentyfold, yet transcription still starts at the same base. What was deleted?
choices: The promoter, where polymerase II assembles
An operator, as found in a bacterial operon
An enhancer, which raises the rate of initiation
A silencer, so expression should have risen instead
questions.explain: Start site unchanged but output down is the signature of a distance element that boosts rate rather than positioning polymerase. Lose the promoter and transcription would not start at that base at all, and losing a repressive element would raise expression.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A solution is made hyperosmotic to plasma by adding urea. Is it hypertonic?
choices: Yes, urea counts as a dissolved solute
No, urea crosses the membrane freely
Only above a urea level of 0.3 Osm
questions.explain: Tonicity counts only the solutes a membrane blocks, so a permeant one raises the osmometer reading without holding water on either side. Treating osmolarity and tonicity as the same number is what makes this look hypertonic.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Cardiac output is calculated as:
choices: Heart rate divided by stroke volume
questions.explain: Beats per minute multiplied by the volume ejected per beat gives a volume per minute, which is the only combination whose units come out as mL/min. Dividing or subtracting leaves a number with no physical meaning.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Renal clearance of a substance equals (urine concentration x urine flow rate) divided by:
questions.explain: Clearance is the volume of plasma that would have to be stripped completely clean each minute to account for the amount appearing in the urine. Dividing by GFR instead gives a dimensionless ratio, not a volume per minute.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: What does ejection fraction measure?
choices: The share of filled volume ejected
Total blood volume pumped each minute
questions.explain: It is a ratio describing pump performance, not a flow, so it carries no volume per minute. Normal sits around 55 to 70 percent, and a low value alongside normal filling points at contractility rather than output.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A right shift of the oxygen dissociation curve means what?
choices: Oxygen is bound more tightly at the heme
Oxygen affinity rises and P50 falls
questions.explain: A right shift is a drop in affinity, so P50 goes up, which is exactly what hard-working tissue needs. Students reverse it because the shift is read as 'more', but the curve's position tracks affinity, not how much oxygen the blood can carry.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Which substance is used to estimate glomerular filtration rate because it is filtered but neither secreted nor reabsorbed?
questions.explain: Only a substance the tubule leaves completely alone lets the amount in urine report the filtered amount directly. Creatinine is the practical clinical stand-in, but it is slightly secreted, so its clearance runs a little above true GFR.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Why does urea contribute little to effective osmolarity across a cell membrane?
choices: It carries no net electrical charge
Its molecules are too large to cross
questions.explain: A solute that equilibrates on both sides can never stay concentrated on one, so it holds no water there. Being uncharged is not the reason: glucose is uncharged too and still counts in full.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: The Bohr effect describes what?
choices: Oxygen binding raises the blood pH
CO2 and acid lower oxygen affinity
Hemoglobin binds CO2 at the heme iron
questions.explain: This page keeps temperature and 2,3-BPG as separate right-shifters, so naming one of those is the usual slip. The real pair binds away from the heme iron and stabilizes the low-affinity T state.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Of the three curves this page plots, which one is drawn with no cooperativity at all?
questions.explain: A Hill coefficient of 1 means binding at one site cannot change any other, which is what a single subunit forces. The S shape of the other two comes from subunits cooperating, not from binding oxygen more tightly.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Of the passive mechanisms on this page, which one saturates?
questions.explain: A carrier changes shape once per molecule, so its cycle time sets a ceiling exactly as an enzyme's does. A channel is an open pore with no per-molecule cycle, so its flux keeps climbing with the gradient.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Cardiac output is 5.4 L/min and heart rate is 72 bpm. What is the stroke volume?
questions.explain: Rearranging the cardiac output formula puts output over rate, and the litres have to become millilitres before the division or the answer lands a thousand times too small. Multiplying the two instead gives a volume no ventricle holds.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A ventricle fills to 150 mL and empties down to 60 mL. What is its ejection fraction?
questions.explain: The stroke volume has to come first, as the difference between the filled and the emptied volume, and only then does it go over the filled volume. Dividing by the 60 mL left behind instead of the 150 mL filled is the usual slip.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Oxygen consumption is 300 mL/min, arterial oxygen content is 200 mL/L and venous content is 140 mL/L. What is the cardiac output by Fick?
questions.explain: The arteriovenous difference is how much oxygen one litre of blood hands over on a single pass, so total consumption over that per-litre delivery gives litres per minute. Adding the two contents instead of subtracting them is the common error.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Urine concentration is 50 mg/mL, urine flow is 2 mL/min and plasma concentration is 0.8 mg/mL. What is the clearance?
questions.explain: Dividing by the plasma concentration is what turns an excretion rate into a volume of plasma cleared, so a plasma value below 1 mg/mL has to push the answer above the raw excretion rate. Multiplying by it drags the answer the wrong way.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: PAH urine concentration is 20 mg/mL, urine flow is 1.5 mL/min and plasma PAH is 0.05 mg/mL. What is the clearance, and what does it estimate?
questions.explain: A plasma concentration in hundredths means the division multiplies the excretion rate by twenty, so dropping that step lands two orders of magnitude low. Filtration alone could not clear this much, which is the clue to which quantity the number reports.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: GFR is 120 mL/min and renal plasma flow is 600 mL/min. What is the filtration fraction?
questions.explain: Filtration fraction is the share of plasma arriving at the glomerulus that actually becomes filtrate, about a fifth, with the rest carrying on to the peritubular capillaries. Flipping the ratio gives plasma flow per unit of filtrate, which is not a fraction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: What is the osmolarity of 0.2 M NaCl, and how does it compare with blood?
choices: 0.20 Osm, which is isotonic to blood
questions.explain: Osmolarity counts particles, so a salt that splits in two doubles the molarity before any comparison with blood's reference 0.30 Osm. Skipping the van't Hoff factor is what makes a concentrated saline look dilute.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Take 0.1 M CaCl2 at 37 degrees C. What are its osmolarity and osmotic pressure?
questions.explain: The particle count enters both lines, the osmolarity and the pressure, and the temperature has to be absolute before it multiplies anything. Leaving the factor out of the pressure line yields exactly a third of the right figure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Myoglobin has a P50 of 2.8 mmHg and a Hill coefficient of 1. What is its saturation at a pO2 of 8.4 mmHg?
questions.explain: With a Hill coefficient of 1 the equation collapses to the pressure over the pressure plus P50, so three times the P50 gives three quarters saturation. Reading 50 percent at any pressure other than the P50 itself is the usual mistake.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: At the placenta maternal and fetal blood both sit at a pO2 of 19 mmHg. Using this page's curves, what are the two saturations?
questions.explain: Each curve passes through half saturation at its own P50 and nowhere else, so the protein with the lower P50 sits higher at any shared pressure. That gap is the whole reason oxygen moves from mother to fetus.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A cell hydrolyzes 30 ATP through its Na/K-ATPase. How many ions move, and what happens to charge?
choices: 60 Na out, 90 K in, net +30 out
90 Na out, 60 K in, no net charge
90 Na out, 60 K in, net +30 out
90 Na in, 60 K out, net +30 in
questions.explain: The ratio per ATP is fixed at three one way and two the other, which is precisely why the charge does not balance and the pump counts as electrogenic. Reversing the directions would destroy the gradients every secondary transporter spends.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A climber at altitude has raised 2,3-BPG and a respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilating. These two push the oxygen curve in opposite directions. What is the effect at the tissues?
choices: Both shifts are Bohr effects, so they cancel at every pO2
The 2,3-BPG right shift wins, unloading is preserved
The alkalosis right shifts it, so unloading improves
The left shift hits loading and unloading alike, both fall
questions.explain: A right shift is lower affinity and a higher P50, and this page lists 2,3-BPG as a right-shifter separate from the Bohr effect proper. Loading happens at the lung's high pressure and unloading at the tissue's low one, so a shift can help at one end without undoing the other.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: Two patients lose half their usable oxygen capacity, one to carbon monoxide and one to anemia. Why is the carbon monoxide patient worse off at the tissues?
choices: Anemia left shifts too, so the two cases behave alike
CO lowers the number of free heme sites and nothing else
CO left shifts the rest, so oxygen is held tightly
CO right shifts the rest, so oxygen is dumped far too early
questions.explain: A left shift is higher affinity, so whatever oxygen is still aboard comes off less readily where it is needed, which is the part losing red cells does not do. The bound gas also raises the remaining subunits' affinity through the same cooperativity that normally helps.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: At the placenta maternal and fetal blood sit at the same pO2, yet fetal blood ends up more saturated. What explains it?
choices: HbF binds 2,3-BPG more tightly, which raises affinity
HbF binds 2,3-BPG weakly, so affinity stays high
HbF has the higher P50, which means tighter binding
Fetal blood simply sits at a higher pO2 than maternal
questions.explain: 2,3-BPG is the molecule that lowers hemoglobin's affinity, so binding it poorly leaves affinity high, which reads as a lower P50 and a leftward curve. A higher P50 would mean the opposite, oxygen given up sooner.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: During a sprint, muscle pO2 falls while local CO2 and acid rise. What does the curve shift add on top of the lower pressure?
choices: The shift raises total capacity, so more oxygen arrives
At that pO2 the curve holds more, so less unloads
The shift only matters in the lung, not in the muscle
At that pO2 the curve holds less, so more unloads
questions.explain: Where the curve sits decides how much oxygen is held at a given pressure, while capacity is set by how much hemoglobin is present. Lower affinity at the tissue end means a bigger fall in saturation across the same drop in pressure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis starts an ACE inhibitor and the GFR falls. What happened at the arterioles?
choices: The afferent arteriole constricted, so RPF and GFR both fell
The efferent dilated, RPF rose while GFR and FF fell
The efferent constricted, so GFR rose and RPF fell
Both arterioles dilated, so GFR and FF rose together
questions.explain: Angiotensin II normally holds the downstream arteriole tight, propping glomerular pressure up when perfusion is poor, so removing it lets blood leave the glomerulus more easily. Filtration fraction is GFR over plasma flow, so it falls when one drops and the other rises.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A lab infuses PAH hard enough to raise plasma PAH well above normal, then computes renal plasma flow from its clearance. What goes wrong?
choices: Secretion saturates, so clearance now reads low
Secretion saturates, so clearance reads too high
Filtration saturates, so clearance now equals GFR
Nothing, the estimate holds at any concentration
questions.explain: The transporters that strip this marker from plasma have a transport maximum, so past it a smaller share leaves per pass and the clearance stops tracking the whole plasma flow. Real measurements are made at deliberately low concentrations for that reason.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.q: A substance clears at 150 mL/min in a patient whose inulin clearance is 125 mL/min. What must its tubular handling include?
choices: Net reabsorption, since clearance sits above GFR
Net secretion on top of what filtration delivers
Filtration alone, since 150 is a normal figure
Neither, the clearance cannot exceed the GFR here
